newsitem.title: CANADA: Shell Canada to sell chemical unit for US$467 million.
newsitem.headline: Shell Canada to sell chemical unit for US$467 million.

text.p: Shell Canada Ltd. said Tuesday it would sell its chemicals division to a unit of its corporate parent, Royal Dutch/Shell Group, for C$635 million ($467 million).
"We have made the decision to exit the chemical business," Shell Canada President Chuck Wilson said.

"While we have a world-scale, competitive styrene facility today, operating in a global chemical business based largely on one plant and one commodity chemical is in the long run an unsustainable position," he said.

The deal, in which an affiliate of London-based Shell International Chemicals Ltd. would acquire a major Alberta styrene plant and isopropyl alcohol facilities in Ontario, was expected to be completed by year-end, the company said.
Shell Canada, 78-percent owned by Royal Dutch/Shell, said it expected the sale to result in a C$200 million ($147 million) after-tax gain.

The sale includes Shell Canada's styrene plant in Fort Saskatchewan, Alberta, and isopropyl alcohol facilties in Sarnia, Ontario, and related marketing operations. The company sold its polypropylene assets in 1995.

Analysts said the division was being sold to Shell International at an extremely favourable price to Shell Canada, given current weakness in the market for styrene, which is used to make plastics such as those in consumer packaging.
"They got a hell of a price for it -- I never would have thought they would have gotten this kind of dollar," said Martin Molyneaux, analyst with FirstEnergy Capital Corp.
Molyneaux estimated the value of the deal at nearly C$4 ($2.92) a Shell Canada share on an after-tax basis, about C$1 (73 cents) a share higher than his estimated value of the assets being sold.

Shell Canada Vice President Ron Blakely said the company's chemicals division was set to contribute C$40 million ($29.2 million) to the company's earnings in 1996, well below the C$221 million ($161.3 million) earned last year.
Much of the drop was due to styrene prices, which have fallen to about 23 cents a pound on the U.S. Gulf Coast from 46 cents a pound in the first quarter of 1995, Blakely said.

He said the chemicals sale was aimed at streamlining Shell Canada's operations, and was not due to any impending sale by Royal Dutch/Shell. Shell Canada sale rumours have circulated in Canada's energy industry for several years.
"To the best of our knowledge, the shareholder has no intention of selling any further interest in the other parts of our business," Blakely said.
"You have to distinguish between this chemical business and it being a global business and the rest of our business, (which) is essentially North American-focused," he said.
In London, a spokesman for Royal Dutch/Shell said on Tuesday the Anglo-Dutch giant would stick to its interest in its Canadian energy arm after the chemical sale.
"The stake remains unchanged: 78 percent owned by Royal Dutch/Shell Group and 22 percent owned by the majority public shareholders," the spokesman said.
With the purchase, Shell International's operations were expected to be better positioned to compete in the world chemicals market, he said.
Canada's second-largest integrated oil company by 1995 revenues, Shell Canada produces oil, gas and sulphur and is a major refiner and gasoline marketer.
Under the sale arrangement, all current Shell Canada chemicals employees were expected to be retained by the new company.
